# 1. Setup and packages

```{r packages}
pkgs <- c("mlbench", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "caret",
          "pROC", "corrplot", "randomForest")
for (p in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}
invisible(lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))
set.seed(123)
```

# 2. Dataset identification

Dataset: `PimaIndiansDiabetes2` from the `mlbench` package (originally from the
National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases). It holds
medical measurements for 768 women of Pima Indian heritage aged 21 or older.
The target is `diabetes` (pos / neg).

```{r load}
df <- NULL

# Try 1: from the mlbench package
df <- tryCatch(mlbench::PimaIndiansDiabetes2, error = function(e) NULL)

# Try 2: download the raw data if the package version fails
if (is.null(df)) {
  df <- tryCatch({
    url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jbrownlee/Datasets/master/pima-indians-diabetes.data.csv"
    d <- read.csv(url, header = FALSE)
    names(d) <- c("pregnant", "glucose", "pressure", "triceps",
                  "insulin", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes")
    d$diabetes <- factor(ifelse(d$diabetes == 1, "pos", "neg"),
                         levels = c("neg", "pos"))
    cols <- c("glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass")
    d[cols] <- lapply(d[cols], function(x) ifelse(x == 0, NA, x))
    d
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
}

if (is.null(df)) stop("Dataset could not be loaded. Install mlbench and restart R.")

df <- as.data.frame(df)
dim(df)
str(df)
head(df)
```

# 3. Exploratory statistical analysis

## 3.1 Summary statistics and missing values

```{r summary}
summary(df)
colSums(is.na(df))
round(colMeans(is.na(df)) * 100, 1)   # % missing per column

miss <- colSums(is.na(df))
barplot(miss, las = 2, col = "steelblue",
        main = "Missing values per variable", ylab = "Count")
```

## 3.2 Target balance

```{r balance}
table(df$diabetes)
round(prop.table(table(df$diabetes)), 3)
ggplot(df, aes(diabetes, fill = diabetes)) + geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Class distribution", x = "Diabetes", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 3.3 Distributions

```{r distributions}
long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(df, cols = -diabetes,
                            names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

ggplot(long, aes(value, fill = diabetes)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of predictors by diabetes status") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(long, aes(diabetes, value, fill = diabetes)) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 3.4 Normality checks

H0: the variable is normally distributed. H1: it is not.

```{r normality}
num_vars <- setdiff(names(df), "diabetes")

normality <- sapply(num_vars, function(v) shapiro.test(na.omit(df[[v]]))$p.value)
round(normality, 6)

par(mfrow = c(2, 4))
for (v in num_vars) {
  qqnorm(df[[v]], main = paste("Q-Q plot:", v))
  qqline(df[[v]], col = "red")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Note: with n = 768 the Shapiro-Wilk test is very sensitive, so Q-Q plots
should be read together with the p-values. Most variables are right-skewed,
which supports using non-parametric tests alongside t-tests.

## 3.5 Correlation analysis

```{r correlation}
num_df  <- df[, num_vars]
cor_mat <- cor(num_df, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
round(cor_mat, 2)
corrplot(cor_mat, method = "color", type = "upper", addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.7, tl.col = "black")

cor.test(df$glucose, df$insulin, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
cor.test(df$age, df$pregnant, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

## 3.6 Hypothesis tests

**Test 1: Is mean glucose different between diabetic and non-diabetic groups?**

- H0: mean glucose (pos) = mean glucose (neg)
- H1: mean glucose (pos) is different from mean glucose (neg)

```{r ttest}
t.test(glucose ~ diabetes, data = df)
wilcox.test(glucose ~ diabetes, data = df, exact = FALSE)
```

**Test 2: The same comparison for every predictor (Wilcoxon rank-sum)**

```{r wilcox-all}
wil <- sapply(num_vars, function(v) {
  wilcox.test(df[[v]] ~ df$diabetes, exact = FALSE)$p.value
})
wil_tbl <- data.frame(variable = num_vars,
                      p_value = signif(wil, 3),
                      p_adj_bonferroni = signif(p.adjust(wil, "bonferroni"), 3))
wil_tbl[order(wil_tbl$p_value), ]
```

**Test 3: Is diabetes associated with age group? (Chi-square)**

- H0: diabetes status is independent of age group
- H1: diabetes status depends on age group

```{r chisq}
age_group <- cut(df$age, breaks = c(20, 30, 40, 50, Inf),
                 labels = c("21-30", "31-40", "41-50", "51+"))
tab <- table(age_group, df$diabetes)
tab
chisq.test(tab)
round(prop.table(tab, 1), 3)
```

**Test 4: Variance check (Levene / Brown-Forsythe style test) for glucose**

```{r levene}
gl <- df[!is.na(df$glucose), ]
gl$abs_dev <- abs(gl$glucose - ave(gl$glucose, gl$diabetes, FUN = median))
anova(lm(abs_dev ~ diabetes, data = gl))
```

# 4. Model building

## 4.1 Train / test split

Missing values are imputed **inside** the cross-validation folds (median
imputation via `preProcess`), which avoids data leakage.

```{r split}
set.seed(123)
idx   <- createDataPartition(df$diabetes, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train <- df[idx, ]
test  <- df[-idx, ]
dim(train); dim(test)
round(prop.table(table(train$diabetes)), 3)
round(prop.table(table(test$diabetes)), 3)
```

## 4.2 Cross-validation setup

```{r control}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                     savePredictions = "final")
# NOTE: for twoClassSummary the first factor level ("neg") is treated as the
# event, so Sens/Spec in the CV table refer to "neg". ROC (AUC) is unaffected.
```

## 4.3 Model 1: Logistic regression

```{r glm}
set.seed(123)
fit_glm <- train(diabetes ~ ., data = train,
                 method = "glm", family = "binomial",
                 metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
                 preProcess = c("medianImpute", "center", "scale"),
                 na.action = na.pass)
fit_glm
summary(fit_glm$finalModel)
```

## 4.4 Model 2: Random forest (comparison model)

```{r rf}
set.seed(123)
fit_rf <- train(diabetes ~ ., data = train,
                method = "rf", metric = "ROC", trControl = ctrl,
                tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 4)),
                ntree = 200,
                preProcess = c("medianImpute"),
                na.action = na.pass)
fit_rf
plot(fit_rf)
```

## 4.5 Cross-validated comparison

```{r compare}
res <- resamples(list(Logistic = fit_glm, RandomForest = fit_rf))
summary(res)
bwplot(res, metric = "ROC")
```

# 5. Evaluation on the held-out test set

```{r test-eval}
pred_glm <- predict(fit_glm, newdata = test, na.action = na.pass)
prob_glm <- predict(fit_glm, newdata = test, type = "prob", na.action = na.pass)[, "pos"]
cm_glm   <- confusionMatrix(pred_glm, test$diabetes, positive = "pos")
cm_glm

pred_rf <- predict(fit_rf, newdata = test, na.action = na.pass)
prob_rf <- predict(fit_rf, newdata = test, type = "prob", na.action = na.pass)[, "pos"]
cm_rf   <- confusionMatrix(pred_rf, test$diabetes, positive = "pos")
cm_rf

metrics <- data.frame(
  Model       = c("Logistic", "RandomForest"),
  Accuracy    = c(cm_glm$overall["Accuracy"],     cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"]),
  Sensitivity = c(cm_glm$byClass["Sensitivity"],  cm_rf$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
  Specificity = c(cm_glm$byClass["Specificity"],  cm_rf$byClass["Specificity"]),
  Precision   = c(cm_glm$byClass["Precision"],    cm_rf$byClass["Precision"]),
  F1          = c(cm_glm$byClass["F1"],           cm_rf$byClass["F1"])
)
metrics[, -1] <- round(metrics[, -1], 3)
metrics
```

## 5.1 Confusion matrix plot

```{r cm-plot}
plot_cm <- function(cm, title) {
  ggplot(as.data.frame(cm$table), aes(Reference, Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
    geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 6) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = title) + theme_minimal()
}
plot_cm(cm_glm, "Logistic regression: confusion matrix")
plot_cm(cm_rf,  "Random forest: confusion matrix")
```

## 5.2 ROC curves and AUC

```{r roc}
roc_glm <- roc(test$diabetes, prob_glm, levels = c("neg", "pos"), direction = "<")
roc_rf  <- roc(test$diabetes, prob_rf,  levels = c("neg", "pos"), direction = "<")
auc(roc_glm); auc(roc_rf)

plot(roc_glm, col = "blue", lwd = 2, main = "ROC curves (test set)")
plot(roc_rf, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c(paste("Logistic AUC =", round(auc(roc_glm), 3)),
                  paste("RF AUC =", round(auc(roc_rf), 3))),
       col = c("blue", "darkgreen"), lwd = 2)
```

# 6. Diagnostic analysis

## 6.1 Logistic regression: odds ratios

Predictors were standardized, so each odds ratio is per 1 standard deviation increase.

```{r odds}
glm_final <- fit_glm$finalModel
ci <- exp(confint.default(glm_final))
or_tbl <- data.frame(
  term       = names(coef(glm_final)),
  odds_ratio = round(exp(coef(glm_final)), 3),
  CI_low     = round(ci[, 1], 3),
  CI_high    = round(ci[, 2], 3),
  p_value    = round(summary(glm_final)$coefficients[, 4], 4)
)
rownames(or_tbl) <- NULL
or_tbl
```

## 6.2 Multicollinearity (VIF, computed manually)

```{r vif}
X <- model.matrix(glm_final)[, -1]
vif_vals <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(X)), function(i) {
  r2 <- summary(lm(X[, i] ~ X[, -i]))$r.squared
  1 / (1 - r2)
})
names(vif_vals) <- colnames(X)
round(vif_vals, 2)    # values above 5 suggest a problem
```

## 6.3 Residual diagnostics

```{r residuals}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(glm_final)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

res_df <- data.frame(fitted  = fitted(glm_final),
                     dev_res = residuals(glm_final, type = "deviance"))
ggplot(res_df, aes(fitted, dev_res)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Deviance residuals vs fitted probabilities",
       x = "Fitted probability", y = "Deviance residual") +
  theme_minimal()

cd <- cooks.distance(glm_final)
plot(cd, type = "h", main = "Cook's distance", ylab = "Cook's D")
abline(h = 4 / length(cd), col = "red", lty = 2)
sum(cd > 4 / length(cd))    # number of potentially influential points
```

## 6.4 Variable importance

```{r varimp}
plot(varImp(fit_glm), main = "Logistic regression: variable importance")
plot(varImp(fit_rf),  main = "Random forest: variable importance")
```

# 7. Optimization and improvement

## 7.1 Threshold tuning (improving sensitivity)

```{r threshold}
best <- coords(roc_glm, "best", best.method = "youden",
               ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))
best

thr <- as.numeric(best[["threshold"]][1])
new_pred <- factor(ifelse(prob_glm >= thr, "pos", "neg"), levels = c("neg", "pos"))
confusionMatrix(new_pred, test$diabetes, positive = "pos")
```

## 7.2 Other ideas to try

- Better imputation (kNN or `mice`) instead of median imputation
- Feature engineering (e.g. BMI categories, glucose x age interaction)
- Class balancing (SMOTE or down-sampling) and tuning with a recall-focused metric
- Other models: regularized logistic regression (glmnet), gradient boosting (xgboost), SVM
- Repeated cross-validation for more stable estimates

```{r values, include=FALSE}
auc_glm  <- as.numeric(auc(roc_glm));  auc_rf  <- as.numeric(auc(roc_rf))
acc_glm  <- as.numeric(cm_glm$overall["Accuracy"])
acc_rf   <- as.numeric(cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"])
sens_glm <- as.numeric(cm_glm$byClass["Sensitivity"])
sens_rf  <- as.numeric(cm_rf$byClass["Sensitivity"])
spec_glm <- as.numeric(cm_glm$byClass["Specificity"])
spec_rf  <- as.numeric(cm_rf$byClass["Specificity"])
baseline <- max(prop.table(table(test$diabetes)))
best_model <- ifelse(auc_glm >= auc_rf, "logistic regression", "random forest")
imp <- varImp(fit_glm)$importance
top_feat <- rownames(imp)[order(-imp$Overall)][1:3]
p_glucose <- t.test(glucose ~ diabetes, data = df)$p.value
p_chisq   <- chisq.test(tab)$p.value
sig_vars  <- wil_tbl$variable[wil_tbl$p_adj_bonferroni < 0.05]
```

# 8. Key Insights

- **Group differences:** After Bonferroni correction, these predictors differed significantly between diabetic and non-diabetic patients: `r paste(sig_vars, collapse = ", ")`.
- **Glucose:** The Welch t-test for glucose gave p = `r format.pval(p_glucose, digits = 3)`, so mean glucose differs between the two groups.
- **Age and diabetes:** The chi-square test of age group vs diabetes gave p = `r format.pval(p_chisq, digits = 3)`.
- **Model performance:** On the test set, logistic regression reached an accuracy of `r round(acc_glm, 3)` and AUC of `r round(auc_glm, 3)`; random forest reached an accuracy of `r round(acc_rf, 3)` and AUC of `r round(auc_rf, 3)`.
- **Baseline comparison:** Always predicting the majority class would give an accuracy of `r round(baseline, 3)`, so the models should be judged against this number.
- **Sensitivity vs specificity:** Logistic regression detected `r round(sens_glm * 100, 1)`% of diabetic cases (specificity `r round(spec_glm * 100, 1)`%); random forest detected `r round(sens_rf * 100, 1)`% (specificity `r round(spec_rf * 100, 1)`%).
- **Best model by AUC:** `r best_model`.

# 9. Key Features

The three most important predictors in the logistic regression model were
**`r top_feat[1]`**, **`r top_feat[2]`** and **`r top_feat[3]`**
(see the variable importance plot in section 6.4). The table below summarizes all features used.

```{r features, echo=FALSE}
feat <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("pregnant", "glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin",
              "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"),
  Description = c("Number of times pregnant",
                  "Plasma glucose concentration (2-hour oral glucose tolerance test)",
                  "Diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg)",
                  "Triceps skin fold thickness (mm)",
                  "2-hour serum insulin (mu U/ml)",
                  "Body mass index",
                  "Diabetes pedigree function",
                  "Age in years",
                  "Target: pos / neg"),
  Type = c(rep("Numeric predictor", 8), "Binary target")
)
knitr::kable(feat)
```

# 10. Conclusion

This project analysed the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset using hypothesis tests,
correlation and normality analysis, and two classification models evaluated with
10-fold cross-validation and a held-out test set. The best-performing model by AUC
was **`r best_model`**, with logistic regression reaching an AUC of
`r round(auc_glm, 3)` and random forest `r round(auc_rf, 3)`.

The statistical tests and the model importance scores point to the same group of
key predictors (`r paste(top_feat, collapse = ", ")`), which supports the validity
of the findings. The main limitations are the small sample size, median
imputation of missing values, and moderate class imbalance. Future work could use
multiple imputation, feature engineering, class balancing, threshold tuning and
other algorithms such as gradient boosting.
